text: Why did the bicycle fall over? It was two-tired.

review.notes: Recycled public-domain joke-book staple ('two-tired'); instantly recognizable and not original to StreakFit.

text: Why don't kettlebells ever tell secrets? They always spill the iron.

review.notes: Punchline substitutes a word without creating a double meaning: 'spill the iron' is not a phrase and iron does not spill. The kettlebell/iron link is there but the idiom swap does no comic work.

text: Why did the jump rope quit its job? It was tired of being skipped.

review.notes: Clean double meaning on 'skipped' (rope-skipping / being passed over); original and warm.

text: Why do stretches make terrible liars? They're always caught reaching.

review.notes: Rests on the adult idiom 'that's a reach' (exaggerating), which a nine-year-old is unlikely to have. The obvious child-legible pun, 'stretch the truth', is sitting right there unused.

text: What's a runner's favorite school subject? Jog-raphy.

review.notes: Generic schoolyard pun that reads as stock; the stress also does not match ('gee-OG-raphy' vs 'JOG-raphy'), so the pun is a beat off when read aloud.

text: What do you call a vegetable that lifts weights? A buff-et.

review.notes: Broken construction: the setup asks for a vegetable and the punchline is a buffet, which is not a vegetable. 'Buffet' is also said 'buh-FAY', so the 'buff' pun does not survive being read aloud.

text: Why did the smoothie blush? It saw the blender's smooth moves.

review.notes: No twist: the punchline just restates 'smoothie' as 'smooth'. Nothing flips meaning, and 'blush' gives the reward line an odd romantic framing for a nine-year-old.

text: What do you call a chicken at the gym? A hen-thusiast.

review.notes: Phonetically clean ('en-thusiast' / 'hen-thusiast'), gettable, no target but the chicken.

text: What's a tree's favorite exercise? Branch presses.

review.notes: Bench press / branch press lands in one beat and is age-legible.

text: Why did the apple join the gym? It wanted to turn over a new leaf.

review.notes: Real double meaning on 'leaf'; mild but sound and warm.

text: Why did the broccoli win the race? It was ahead by a sprout.

review.notes: Factual mismatch breaks the pun: broccoli has florets, not sprouts. The joke wants a Brussels sprout, or the vegetable needs changing.

text: Why don't oranges ever skip leg day? They're always well-rounded.

review.notes: 'Well-rounded' carries both the shape and the training sense; the leg-day framing stays about the orange, not about anyone's body.

text: What's a fish's favorite workout? The backstroke.

review.notes: No joke mechanism at all: 'the backstroke' is a literal, expected answer for a fish. Setup and punchline are the same thought with no twist or wordplay.

text: Why did the stairs get a promotion? They always stepped up.

review.notes: 'Stepped up' works in both senses; short, sound, quietly charming.

text: What do you call a calm cucumber? Cool, collected, and well-hydrated.

review.notes: Punchline is a bland positive statement with no wordplay or twist. 'Cool as a cucumber' is a worn idiom and the line never even completes it.

text: Why did the egg go for a jog? It wanted to get a little more egg-cited.

review.notes: 'Egg-cited' is a tired staple, and the setup does not set it up: jogging has no connection to excitement, so the two halves are unrelated.

text: Why did the pillow join the wellness club? It needed better support.

review.notes: 'Support' genuinely means two things here; gentle and in voice. 'Wellness club' is slightly stiff phrasing but works.

text: What do you call a dog that does yoga? A dog-a practitioner.

review.notes: The pun never lands on the page: 'dog-a practitioner' needs the reader to supply 'yoga', and the word 'yoga' already appears in the setup, so the joke is just the word restated with a hyphen.

text: Why did the watermelon win an award? It was outstanding in its field.

review.notes: Recycled public-domain joke ('outstanding in his field', normally the scarecrow or the corn) with the fruit swapped in. Recognizable to almost every adult reader.

text: Why did the salad get the lead role? It really dressed the part.

review.notes: Salad dressing / dressing the part is a real double meaning, and the theatre setup is a fresh frame for it.

text: What do plants say after a workout? "That was un-be-leaf-able!"

review.notes: 'Un-be-leaf-able' is a widely circulated stock pun, and nothing about a workout makes plants say it: the setup and punchline are unconnected.

text: What's a frog's favorite exercise? Jumping jacks.

review.notes: No twist: frogs jump, so 'jumping jacks' is the literal expected answer, not a punchline. Also one of the most-told kids' joke staples.

text: Why did the grape stop exercising? It was raisin the bar too high.

review.notes: Raisin / raising is clean and gettable, and setting the bar too high is an idea this app's readers will recognize in themselves.

text: What do you call a well-rested mountain? Boulder than ever.

review.notes: Boulder / bolder lands cleanly; the rest-to-bold link is loose but readable.

text: Why did the tomato turn red? It saw the salad getting all the attention.

review.notes: A mangled version of the famous 'it saw the salad dressing' joke: the original pun has been removed and replaced with jealousy over attention, which is both unfunny and a comparison between two characters rather than a wordplay.

text: Why did the lemon stay positive? It always looked for the zest in life.

review.notes: Zest / best works in one beat and is age-legible.

text: What do you call a strong bowl of soup? Souper fit.

review.notes: 'Souper' is one of the most worn puns in circulation, and 'souper fit' is not a phrase the pun transforms; there is no second meaning, only a respelling.

text: What do you call a chill mushroom? A fungi who knows how to relax.

review.notes: Leans on the single most famous mushroom joke ('a fun guy') but never lands it: the punchline says 'fungi' and then explains relaxation in plain words, so the reader does all the work and gets a joke they already know.

text: Why did the bread feel proud after baking? It really rose to the occasion.

review.notes: 'Rose to the occasion' is familiar but genuinely double-meaning here, and the pride framing is on-voice.

text: What do you call a strong cup of tea? A steeped-up workout buddy.

review.notes: Near-duplicate of SF-JOK-000014, which already uses 'stepped up'. 'A steeped-up workout buddy' is also not an idiom, so the pun has nothing to bounce off.

text: What do you call a happy, hydrated flower? Well-watered and blooming.

review.notes: Not a joke: the punchline is a bland positive statement ('well-watered and blooming') with no wordplay, twist or surprise of any kind.

text: What's a turtle's favorite exercise? Slow and steady stretching.

review.notes: No punchline: 'slow and steady stretching' is the literal expected answer for a turtle, and 'slow and steady' is a stock phrase used straight.

text: What do you call a strong loaf of bread? Well-kneaded.

review.notes: The 'kneaded/needed' pun is never activated, so the line reads as a literal baking description; it also repeats the bread subject already used in SF-JOK-000029.

text: Why did the raccoon do push-ups? Bin lids are heavier than they look.

review.notes: The strongest item in the packet: in character, self-deprecating, original, and the humour is entirely at the raccoon's expense.

text: What do you call a relaxed cactus? Low maintenance and well-grounded.

review.notes: Not a joke: a bland positive description of a cactus with no twist. 'Well-grounded' is also reused verbatim in SF-JOK-000044.

text: What's a snail's favorite kind of workout? Anything nice and slow.

review.notes: No wordplay and no surprise: 'nice and slow' is the literal expected answer for a snail. Near-identical in shape and idea to SF-JOK-000032.

text: What do you call a happy glass of water? Refreshed and ready for more.

review.notes: Not a joke at all: a bland affirmation with no setup-payoff relationship. Occupies a reader's one reward slot for the day and gives nothing back.

text: Why did the banana feel great after the walk? It was finally peeling good.

review.notes: The construction is fine but 'peeling good' is an extremely well-worn staple that most readers will have met already; needs a fresher turn on the banana.

text: Why did the celery look so fit? It always stayed crunchy and upright.

review.notes: Two faults: there is no pun, only a literal description; and the setup judges by how something 'looks so fit', which is exactly the appearance framing this content must avoid.

text: What do you call a strong, steady walk? A step in the right direction.

review.notes: Not a joke: 'a step in the right direction' is a motivational cliche delivered straight, with no second meaning beyond the one everybody already uses.

text: Why did the balloon skip the gym? It already felt light and full of air.

review.notes: The punchline rewards skipping the workout, which is the wrong message on a completion screen, and the available pun ('full of hot air') is never actually made.

text: What do you call a calm wave at the beach? Totally board with stress.

review.notes: The board/bored pun produces a phrase that means nothing: being 'bored with stress' is not a thing, and a wave is not a board, so the substitution has no anchor.

text: Why did the clock stretch every morning? To keep good time with its joints.

review.notes: The pun does not exist: clocks have hands, not joints, so 'keep good time with its joints' joins a clock idiom to a body part the clock does not have. A non-sequitur in a joke's shape.

text: What do you call a carrot that works out? Well-grounded and crunchy strong.

review.notes: No wordplay, just adjectives ('well-grounded and crunchy strong', which is not even grammatical), and 'well-grounded' duplicates SF-JOK-000035.

text: Why did the marathon runner bring a map? To find the long way to feeling great.

review.notes: Non-sequitur: a map has nothing to do with 'the long way to feeling great', and the punchline is a bland positive sentiment rather than a twist.

text: What do you call a happy pair of running shoes? Sole mates.

review.notes: The sole/soul pun is real and gettable at nine, but it is a very well-worn stock pun (shoe-shop slogan level), and the setup does not earn it: 'happy' has nothing to do with being mates. Rewrite the setup around two shoes that go everywhere together, or drop it as recycled.

text: Why did the avocado feel zen after yoga? It found its inner pit of calm.

review.notes: There is a genuine idea (avocado pit / inner peace), but the wording 'inner pit of calm' breaks the sound-echo that makes it a pun — 'peace' never appears, so the payoff is a substitution rather than a twist. Also 'zen' is a reference a nine-year-old may not have. Tighten so the pit/peace collision is the punchline and swap 'zen' for a plainer word.

text: What do you call a strong, calm ocean? Well-balanced and full of good vibes.

review.notes: Question-shaped affirmation, not a joke. 'Well-balanced and full of good vibes' is a bland positive restatement of 'strong, calm' in the setup — no wordplay, twist or misdirection. 'Good vibes' also is not Rickie's voice.

text: Why did the spinach feel unstoppable? It always had a leafy green attitude.

review.notes: No joke. 'Leafy green attitude' is just a literal description of spinach glued to the word 'attitude'; the payoff restates the setup's 'unstoppable' with no turn. Gestures at 'can-do attitude' without ever landing the pun.

text: What do you call a peaceful nap after a long walk? A well-earned recharge.

review.notes: Question-shaped affirmation. 'A well-earned recharge' is the literal expected answer to 'a peaceful nap after a long walk' — zero misdirection. Also part of the packet's 'well-' filler-adjective cluster.

text: Why did the cyclist carry a spare inner tube? Because hope is not a repair kit.

review.notes: An actual joke: the setup asks a practical question and the punchline lands a dry aphorism that reframes it. 'Hope is not a repair kit' is original, in Rickie's wry register, safe, and understandable to a nine-year-old who knows bikes get flat tyres.

text: What do you call a flexible willow tree? Bendy, balanced, and proud of it.

review.notes: Question-shaped affirmation with no wordplay — 'bendy, balanced' merely repeats 'flexible' from the setup. Near-duplicate of SF-JOK-000058 (rubber band / 'flexible and ready for anything'); the two cannot both stand.

text: Why did the granola bar feel confident? It was packed with good energy.

review.notes: Bland positive statement, not a punchline. 'Packed with good energy' is the literal thing a granola bar is advertised as; the faint double sense of 'packed' is never activated by the setup.

text: What do you call a calm, steady heartbeat after a walk? A job well done.

review.notes: Weakest structure in the packet: 'A job well done' is not even an answer to 'what do you call a...' — it is a compliment, not a name. Pure affirmation, no joke, and it breaks its own riddle grammar.

text: Why did the orange peel stay positive? It always saw the bright side.

review.notes: The orange/brightness link is the one thread of wordplay, but as written the payoff is the stock phrase 'saw the bright side' with no twist, and 'peel' is arbitrary — the peel has no bearing on optimism. Rebuild around something only a peel can do (zest, getting peeled, being the outside layer) so the pun is the point.

text: What do you call a strong handshake after a workout? A grip well earned.

review.notes: Question-shaped affirmation; 'a grip well earned' just relabels the setup. Third use of the 'well-earned / well done' filler in this packet (see 000050, 000054), so it also reads as template fatigue.

text: Why did the cloud feel lighter after the rain? It let go of what it didn't need.

review.notes: Not a gag but a genuine warm aside, and it earns its place: 'lighter' is true of the cloud literally and of the reader figuratively, so the payoff reframes the setup instead of restating it. Safe, plain language, no one is the butt of it.

text: What do you call a well-stretched rubber band? Flexible and ready for anything.

review.notes: Question-shaped affirmation and a near-duplicate of SF-JOK-000052 (willow tree): both answer a stretchiness setup with 'flexible/bendy... ready for anything'. Also uses the 'well-' filler adjective for the fourth time in the packet.

text: Why did the river keep moving? It liked the steady flow of a good routine.

review.notes: The setup asks a real question and the answer is a habit-app platitude about 'a good routine'. 'Steady flow' is literally true of a river, so nothing turns; it reads as the product's own messaging wearing a joke's clothes.

text: What do you call a happy, well-rested raccoon? Rickie, probably.

review.notes: Small but real turn: the expected answer is an adjective and instead it is Rickie himself, with 'probably' doing dry, unshowy work. On-character, warm, self-directed, safe at nine. Note it is the fifth 'What do you call a...' opener and reuses 'well-', so it should be spaced far from the others in rotation.
